analysis.one_liner: Replaces Medicare and Social Security guarantees with private accounts and vouchers, and repeals corporate and estate taxes.
analysis.headline: Paul Ryan's 2008 plan to overhaul health care, Social Security, and taxes never received a committee vote in any of the five House committees it was sent to, and expired when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced Medicare for future retirees with a fixed payment to buy private insurance, let workers divert Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts, and converted Medicaid into block grants while ending the children's health insurance program. On taxes, it would have repealed the corporate income tax, the estate tax, and taxes on capital gains, dividends, and interest, replacing part of that with a consumption-style business tax. It also offered a refundable tax credit to help the uninsured buy coverage and let insurers sell plans across state lines under another state's rules.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and investors, through the permanent elimination of taxes on capital gains, dividends, interest, and estates [S2]. Corporations, through repeal of the corporate income tax in favor of a border-adjustable business consumption tax [S2]. Financial firms, which would manage the new personal Social Security savings accounts [S2]. Health insurers, which would receive the refundable coverage credit and gain the ability to sell individual policies across state lines under the laws of whichever state they chose [S2] [S3]. A narrower benefit flows to uninsured Americans: a refundable credit of $2,500 per adult and $1,000 per child, capped at $5,000 per family, to buy insurance [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, corporations, insurers, and asset managers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable health insurance tax credit of $2,500 per adult and $1,000 per child, up to $5,000 per family, with advance payments sent directly to insurers, aimed at the uninsured [S2] [S3].
Fully repeals the alternative minimum tax, which increasingly reached middle-income taxpayers, and lets individuals elect a simplified two-rate income tax [S2].
Sets rules allowing small businesses to band together in association health plans regulated at the federal level rather than under each state's insurance rules [S2] [S3].
Creates personal Social Security savings accounts that participants could pass on to heirs, and gradually raises the normal retirement age to 67 to restore solvency [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Future Medicare beneficiaries, who would face a higher eligibility age and a new fixed-payment structure for those retiring in 2019 or later, plus income-based reductions in the drug-benefit subsidy [S2]. Medicaid and children's health coverage: states would have to choose block grants or a tax-credit system for acute care, hospital payments would phase out, and the SCHIP program would be abolished [S2]. Workers choosing the new system would see employer-provided health coverage become taxable income, and their guaranteed Social Security benefits reduced in favor of market risk [S2] [S3]. The bill's spending-cap machinery would require automatic cuts if outlays exceeded a set share of the economy [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Future seniors, Medicaid and SCHIP recipients, workers

drawbacks.text: It would abolish the State Children's Health Insurance Program entirely, ending that coverage for low-income children [S2].
It would raise the Medicare eligibility age and shift future retirees from guaranteed Medicare to a defined payment, leaving them exposed to health cost inflation faster than the payment grows [S2].

It would let insurers sell individual policies governed by another state's laws, exempting them from most consumer protections, benefit mandates, and rate rules of the state where the buyer lives; the bill's own required disclosure warns the policy may be cheaper because it skips the home state's mandated benefits [S3].
It would direct Social Security contributions into personal investment accounts, replacing a guaranteed benefit with market risk for participating workers [S2].

It would eliminate taxes on capital gains, dividends, interest, and estates, cutting revenue concentrated among the highest-income households, and replace the corporate income tax with a business consumption tax, shifting the tax base toward consumption [S2].
Its automatic spending-reduction orders and limits on revenue as a share of the economy would force cuts or block new spending whenever the caps were exceeded [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The plan offers real relief to two groups — the uninsured (a capped tax credit) and taxpayers hit by the alternative minimum tax — but the largest and most certain benefits flow to investors, corporations, and the financial industry, while the costs fall on programs that guarantee health and retirement security for seniors and low-income families: SCHIP abolished, Medicaid block-granted, Medicare eligibility raised and converted to a fixed payment, and Social Security partly shifted into individual accounts. The across-state-lines insurance provision would lower premiums for some buyers by stripping the consumer protections of their own state. It is a large, coherent restructuring whose benefits and costs land on very different people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Paul Ryan introduced the Roadmap for America's Future Act on May 21, 2008 [S5].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Rules, and Budget committees [S5].
No committee took action on the bill, and it received no vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the existing Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and children's health guarantees remained intact for the people who rely on them; no industry gained the new subsidies and deregulation the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and SCHIP

for.name: Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which bundled his proposals on health care, Social Security, taxes, and budget controls into one plan.

for.name: 8 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee receiving the primary referral (Democratic majority)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; the committee record shows referral and no further action.

against.name: House Democratic majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee schedules and the House floor in the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Brought the bill no closer to a vote than committee referral over the remaining months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and no committee chaired by the Democratic majority ever considered the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill routes its health coverage subsidy as tax credits paid to private insurers, making them the permanent channel for help to the uninsured, while letting them sell policies across state lines exempt from most consumer protections, benefit mandates, and rate regulation of the buyer's state [S2] [S3].

The corporate income tax is repealed and replaced with a business consumption tax, and taxes on capital gains and dividends are eliminated, concentrating the tax benefit among owners and investors [S2].

industries.industry: Asset managers and financial services firms
industries.note: Personal Social Security savings accounts would channel payroll contributions into individually owned investment accounts, creating a large new pool of fee-earning assets for the financial industry [S2].
The estate tax is repealed and interest income is excluded from tax alongside capital gains and dividends — tax benefits that accrue overwhelmingly at the top of the income distribution [S2].
Disproportionate share hospital payments, which compensate hospitals treating uninsured and Medicaid patients, would be phased out as Medicaid moved to block grants [S2].
States would be forced to choose between capped block grants for acute and long-term care or a tax-credit system replacing parts of Medicaid, shifting cost growth risk onto state budgets [S2].
